abstract: Stereopsis involves combining different views from the two eyes to infer depth, an ability that has intrigued neuroscientists for almost two centuries (Wheatstone, 1838). It enables insects such as the praying mantis to estimate the distance of prey (Nityananda et al., 2018), or primates to fixate objects at different depths (Cumming and Judge, 1986; Rashbass and Westheimer, 1961). While theoretical models for stereopsis have been proposed based on neural activity recordings (Marr and Poggio, 1976; Grossberg, 1983; Ohzawa et al., 1990), we do not have a detailed circuit mechanism for stereopsis founded on neural wiring. Here we achieve this in the fly, Drosophila melanogaster, by analyzing two whole-brain connectomes (Dorkenwald et al., 2024; Berg et al., 2026). Flies have sufficient overlap between the eyes to utilize binocular vision (Kemppainen et al., 2022); however, a circuit that performs stereopsis has not been uncovered in this model system. We show that a cell type that connects the two optic lobes called LC14 (Otsuna and Ito, 2006) forms a recurrent circuit across the brain that is capable of depth estimation. By building a connectome-constrained model, we demonstrate that recurrence is critical for binocular distance tuning in this circuit. Tuning is optimal for the size and distances of social targets (other flies), and we uncover a pathway within the brain specific for binocular vision computations. Silencing LC14 neurons renders this downstream circuitry sensitive to only monocular information and alters distance-dependent courtship behaviors, while activation of LC14 neurons causes flies to slow in response to an illusory object in their binocular visual field. In sum, we predict function from structure, uncovering how the fly brain computes distance from binocular cues, and identify a role for binocular vision in patterning social behavior.
hook: Fly brain wiring shows how two eyes give depth: a loop of LC14 neurons computes distance.
hook_turn: a loop of LC14 neurons computes distance.
summary: Using two whole-brain wiring maps of the fruit fly, researchers found that LC14 neurons linking the two optic lobes form a recurrent loop that can estimate distance. A connectome-based model, plus silencing and activating these cells, linked the circuit to distance-dependent courtship and slowing. The depth tuning comes largely from modeling, not direct recording.
title: A neural circuit for stereopsis in the fly
